A paragraph-wise response, your own account of the facts, the documents that support it, and a clear position on what you are willing to do.
Reference — the notice's date, its reference number and the sender's name. Paragraph-wise reply — number each answer to match the notice. Your version — facts with dates and documents, in a separate section with a heading. Legal position — the sections or clauses you rely on, only if you are sure of them. Offer or refusal — say plainly whether you will pay, perform or deny, and on what terms. Reservation — that all rights and defences are reserved, and that the reply is without prejudice where that is genuinely intended. Proof of dispatch — keep the postal receipt and acknowledgement card.

### What should a reply never do?
Never ignore it, never admit a debt you have not verified, never threaten, and never send it without proof of dispatch.
Ignoring the notice — silence is often read as acceptance in commercial disputes. Emotional language — the reply will be read in court years later; keep it factual. Admitting liability casually — an admission can be used against your client. Raising every defence at once — inconsistent defences weaken the strong one. No proof of service — a reply that cannot be shown to have been received is of little use. Practical note: many cheque cases turn on whether the notice of demand was properly served. Preserve the receipt, the tracking record and the returned envelope.

### How long does the sender have to file after the notice?
It depends on the statute behind the notice. For a dishonoured cheque under 489-F PPC practice, timing of the notice and the complaint matters; for civil claims, limitation runs from the cause of action.
Do not rely on a general figure. Check: The statute named in the notice, and whether it prescribes a period. The limitation applicable to the underlying claim in the Limitation Act 1908. The date of service , not the date of the letter.

Q: Should I reply to a legal notice if the claim is false?
A: Yes. A short, specific denial with your documents is far safer than silence, which can be used to support the sender's story.

Q: Can I reply myself without a lawyer?
A: You can send a factual reply, but a badly worded admission can cost more than the fee. Have a lawyer read the notice before you answer it.

Q: Does a reply stop the other side from going to court?
A: No. It sets out your position, which may encourage settlement, but the sender can still file. The reply becomes part of the record.


## Cause List Tracking for Pakistani Lawyers
URL: https://sarmads050.github.io/wakeelbano/career/cause-list-tracking/

A cause list is the court's daily schedule of cases. Track it by checking the official court source for your court every evening, matching your case register against it, and confirming the result of each hearing the same day. Never depend on a client or a colleague to tell you a date.

- What it is: The court's list of cases fixed for a particular day
- Where published: Official court websites, court notice boards, and the bar association's list
- When to check: The evening before, and again in the morning before appearing
- Core tool: Your own case register: file number, next date, purpose, court, fee status
- Cost of a missed date: Costs, ex parte orders, warrants, or dismissal for non-prosecution
- Best practice: One source of truth, updated daily, backed up
### Where are cause lists published in Pakistan?
Official court websites publish daily and weekly cause lists; district courts rely heavily on notice boards and the bar association's list, and court staff can confirm a fixed date.
Sindh High Court — daily cause lists are published on the court's official website, normally in the evening for the next working day. District and City Courts — printed lists on the notice board, plus the list circulated at the bar room. Confirm with the reader or the court office. Supreme Court — cause lists are published on the Supreme Court website for each bench. Special courts and tribunals — check with the office directly; publication online is not guaranteed. Verification rule: treat any date received by WhatsApp as unconfirmed until you have seen it on the official list or been told by the court office. Screenshots get edited and forwarded with the wrong date.

### How do you read a cause list quickly?
Find your court and bench first, then scan for the case number — not the party names, which are often spelled inconsistently.
Confirm the court, bench and judge heading. The same case can appear before a different bench. Search the case number and year , then cross-check the parties. Note the serial number , the purpose (arguments, evidence, order) and the time slot if shown. Mark whether the matter is listed as fixed or in the supplementary list, which is often heard later in the day. Write the serial number on your file cover before you leave the chamber.

### What should a simple case register contain?
One line per case with the court, file number, parties, next date, purpose, fee position and what happened at the last hearing.
Column Why it matters Court, bench, judge Decides where you stand at 9 a.m. File and case number, year The only reliable identifier in a cause list Parties, short form Quick recognition under time pressure Next date and purpose Drives the evening check Last order, one line Prevents repeating an argument already decided Fee and payment status Stops you appearing on an unpaid brief Documents due Ensures the file is complete before the date A spreadsheet is enough. The point is one register, updated the same day, not five notebooks and a phone gallery.

### What is a workable daily routine?
Evening: check tomorrow's lists against the register. Morning: re-check, then report each hearing result before you leave court.
6 p.m. — open the official list for each court where you have a matter tomorrow. 6.30 p.m. — update the register, message the client the time and court, and prepare the file the night before. 8.30 a.m. — re-check the supplementary list before entering the courtroom. After each hearing — write the one-line order and the next date in the register, not on a loose paper. Weekly — back up the register and review matters with no date for more than 30 days.

Q: What happens if a lawyer misses a hearing?
A: The court may pass an ex parte order, dismiss the matter for non-prosecution, issue warrants, or impose costs. Recovery usually needs an application for restoration or recall, which costs time and money.

Q: Can a client check the cause list themselves?
A: They can read the public list, but the responsibility for tracking stays with the advocate. Set the expectation at the first meeting: dates are confirmed by the chamber, not by rumour.

Q: Is there one app for all Pakistani cause lists?
A: No single official app covers every court. Practitioners use the individual court websites plus their own register. Any third-party app should be treated as a convenience, never as the source of truth.


## Lawyer CV Format for Pakistan
URL: https://sarmads050.github.io/wakeelbano/career/lawyer-cv-format/

A Pakistani legal CV should fit on one page: name and contact, bar enrollment status, education with grades, internships described by what you did, drafting and research skills, languages, and two referees. Chambers hire on demonstrated work, not adjectives.

- Length: One page for students and juniors; two only after five years
- Order: Contact, enrollment status, education, experience, skills, languages, referees
- What wins interviews: Specific drafting and court exposure, with numbers
- What loses them: Generic phrases such as hardworking, and no dates
- Attach: A short covering note and, if asked, two writing samples
### What should a one-page legal CV contain?
Contact details, enrollment or Law-GAT status, education, internships with real descriptions, skills with evidence, languages, and referees.
Header — name, city, phone, professional email, LinkedIn URL. No photo unless asked. Status line — one line: LLB (year, university), Law-GAT status, Sindh Bar Council enrollment number if issued. Education — degree, institution, year, and grades if they are good. Legal experience — internships and pupillage: chamber or firm, court, dates, and what you drafted or observed. Skills — drafting, research databases, court filing, language, typing speed in Urdu and English. Extras — moots, publications, legal aid work, positions held. Referees — two, with designation and a working phone number, and their permission.

### How do you describe an internship properly?
Use verbs and objects: what you drafted, for which court, how many, and under whose supervision.
Weak Strong Worked in a law chamber and learned a lot Drafted 14 bail applications and 6 legal notices for a criminal practice at City Courts, Karachi; maintained a daily cause-list register for 40 files Did research work Prepared case-law memos on 489-F PPC and 497 CrPC, verifying every citation against PLD and SCMR volumes Good communication skills Drafted client correspondence in English and Urdu; translated a 12-page agreement for filing Rule: if a line cannot be proved in an interview with a document or a story, delete it.

### What gets a junior CV rejected?
No dates, unexplained gaps, invented experience, blurry formatting, and applying to chambers whose practice area is nowhere in the CV.
Targeting nothing — a criminal chamber reads a CV full of corporate tax work and moves on. Vague claims — every senior has heard I am a hardworking quick learner. No writing sample — if you claim drafting, keep two samples ready. Careless errors — a misspelt court name or a wrong case citation ends the conversation. Wrong email — a casual address costs interviews. Use name-based email.

Q: Should a fresh graduate include a photo on a legal CV?
A: Usually not. Pakistani legal employers focus on education, drafting exposure and references. Keep the page clean and let the content speak.

Q: Is it acceptable to email chambers directly?
A: Yes. Keep the email to four lines: who you are, what you want, what you offer, and the attached CV. Then follow up once, in person, with a printed copy.

Q: How long should a covering email be?
A: Four to six lines. Seniors read on a phone between hearings. State your university, your enrollment status and which days you are available.


## Your First 30 Days in a Chamber
URL: https://sarmads050.github.io/wakeelbano/career/first-30-days-in-chamber/

In your first 30 days, learn the court routine, build a personal precedent file, volunteer for drafting, and keep a written record of everything you did. Usefulness earns a stipend faster than waiting for one.

- Week 1: Court geography, filing counter, cause list, chamber routine
- Week 2: Read five complete files end to end and summarise each
- Week 3: Draft three documents and have them corrected in red
- Week 4: Ask for one independent task and deliver it early
- Keep forever: A precedent file of your own corrected drafts
- Mistake to avoid: Sitting silent, waiting to be taught
### Week 1 — what should you learn first?
Where things are and how the day runs: the courtrooms, the filing counter, the reader's office, the cause list, and the chamber's own routine.
Walk the court complex with a clerk. Learn the filing counter, the copying agency, the stamp vendor and the library. Ask which court the chamber appears in most, and read three days of cause lists for it. Learn the chamber's filing system and never return a file to the wrong shelf. Write down names and roles: reader, clerk, naib qasid, court stenographer. Arrive before your senior, every day, in the first month.

### Week 2 — how do you learn from files?
Read five complete files end to end, then write a one-page summary of each: parties, facts, stage, next date, and the weak point.
Take a file that has reached arguments, not a brand-new one. Read the plaint or FIR, the reply, the orders and the last application. Write the chronology yourself — do not copy the senior's note. Identify the single weakest link in the case and say why. Compare your note with the senior's and ask what you missed. Why this works: in six months you will have read a hundred files and written a hundred summaries. That record is worth more to an employer than your transcript.

### Week 3 — how do you start drafting?
Copy the structure, not the facts. Draft by hand, get it corrected, and keep the corrected version in your own precedent file.
Ask for a document you have seen before: a legal notice, an application for adjournment, a bail application. Draft from the file, never from a template with someone else's facts left inside. Submit with a note of the points you were unsure about — seniors respect flagged doubts. Keep the corrected draft. Highlight every change you did not expect. Never file anything you have not read end to end yourself.

### Week 4 — how do you become paid, not just present?
Ask for one task you can own completely, deliver it early, and then ask directly about the terms of your seat.
Volunteer for a research memo, a set of case summaries or a cause-list register. Deliver a day before the deadline, with sources checked. Ask for feedback in one question: what would make this usable as filed? At the end of the month, ask about hours, stipend and what you will be taught. Put the agreed terms in writing — even a short WhatsApp message that the senior confirms. Reality check: many chambers in Karachi pay nothing for the first months. Decide in advance how long you can sustain that, and plan the work-board income that covers the gap.

Q: Should a pupil ask for a stipend in the first month?
A: Not usually in the first week, but by the end of the first month it is reasonable to ask about terms. Ask in a scheduled conversation, not in the corridor, and be clear about what you are already delivering.

Q: What if the chamber gives no work at all?
A: Ask for specific work, and give a deadline you control. If nothing changes after six weeks, the seat is not a training seat, and it is reasonable to look elsewhere without burning the relationship.

Q: How many hours should a junior expect to work?
A: Court hours plus chamber hours, typically six days a week in a litigation practice. Agree the expectations in writing so that both sides know what the first year looks like.


## Lawyer Chamber for Rent in Karachi
URL: https://sarmads050.github.io/wakeelbano/karachi/chamber-seat-rent/

A shared chamber seat in Karachi usually costs Rs 6,000 to 15,000 a month, depending on the court vicinity, the size of the chamber and whether a clerk is included. Always agree in writing what the seat includes before paying.

- Typical seat share: Rs 6,000 to 15,000 a month
- Usually included: Desk, chair, cupboard, electricity, and shared use of the library
- Often extra: Clerk's salary, stationery, internet, chamber maintenance
- Best locations: Around City Courts, Saddar, Garden and near the Sindh High Court
- Usual arrangement: Two or three juniors share one chamber and split the rent
- Written record needed: Rent, inclusions, notice period, and who holds the key
### What does a chamber seat actually cost?
Between Rs 6,000 and Rs 15,000 a month for a shared seat, with the higher end near the High Court and in chambers with a library and clerk.
Arrangement Typical monthly cost What you get Desk in a shared chamber Rs 6,000 – 9,000 Desk, chair, cupboard, shared library Seat plus clerk support Rs 10,000 – 15,000 Adds filing, copying and cause-list help Small independent chamber Rs 20,000 and above Own room, often with utilities separate Figures are indicative for 2026 and vary street to street. Treat them as a starting point for negotiation, not a rate card.

### What should a junior check before sharing a chamber?
Who the tenant of record is, what the rent includes, how the key is held, whether the senior is present daily, and whether client files will be safe.
Tenancy — the chamber's own lease and the person legally entitled to sublet space. Inclusions — electricity, internet, cleaning, clerk, stationery. Get a list, not a promise. Security — a locker or cupboard you alone can lock, and a written inventory. Use of the library — borrowing rules, and whether reports may leave the chamber. Notice — how many days must either side give before leaving. Client meetings — whether you may meet your own clients there, and at what hours. Do not pay a deposit without a receipt that names the payer, the amount, the period covered and what the deposit secures.

### How does seat sharing between juniors work in practice?
Two or three juniors take one chamber, split the rent and utilities, and agree a rota for who receives clients and how files are stored.
Agree the split in writing: rent, utilities, clerk, stationery. Allocate desks and storage physically, so nothing is ambiguous. Set rules on client meetings — booked slots, no overlapping appointments. Keep separate files, in separately locked cupboards. Fix an exit clause: 30 days' notice, deposit returned after the final utility bill.

### Is a chamber seat worth the money in the first year?
Yes, if it puts you within walking distance of your court and gives you a place clients can visit. It is a cost of doing business, not a luxury.
Compare it with the alternative: Working from home means no walk-in clients and no library. Paying for a separate room costs two to three times more for the same utility. A shared seat near the court saves travel time, which is the scarcest resource of a junior. On a Rs 30,000 stipend, a Rs 8,000 seat is 27% of income — but it is the difference between being a lawyer with an address and one without.

Q: Can a chamber seat be shared by a man and a woman advocate?
A: Shared professional space is a matter for the parties to agree, and many chambers allocate separate desks and storage. What matters is a written arrangement that both sides are comfortable with; harassment at the workplace is separately governed by law.

Q: Do I need a separate chamber to take my own clients?
A: No, but you need a place where a client can sit and where your files are safe. Confirm with your senior or co-sharers that you may meet your own clients there.

Q: What is a fair deposit for a chamber seat?
A: Commonly one month's rent. Anything higher should be justified in writing and covered by a receipt that states the terms of return.


## Karachi City Courts: A Guide for New Lawyers
URL: https://sarmads050.github.io/wakeelbano/karachi/city-courts-guide/

The City Courts complex in Karachi is where most civil, criminal and family trials begin. New lawyers should learn the filing counter, the cause list, the courtrooms of their own cases and basic courtroom etiquette before anything else.

- What sits here: Civil, criminal, family and miscellaneous trial matters
- Main tasks: Filing, scrutiny, cause list, appearances, copies of orders
- First week goal: Know the filing counter, the copying agency and your courtrooms
- Carry daily: CNIC, bar card, vakalatnamas, court fee stamps, diary, cause list
- Timing: Arrive before the court sits; the list is called early
- Local rules: Filing requirements and scrutiny objections vary by court — read the notice board
### What happens at the filing counter?
Your plaint or application is presented, checked for court fee and annexures, and either registered or returned with objections.
Complete the court fee and stamp requirements before you reach the counter. Keep the plaint or petition, annexures, vakalatnama and identity documents in one tagged set. Present the file; the office checks pagination, court fee and the list of documents. If objections are raised, note them exactly and clear them the same day — do not wait for the next date. Collect the receipt or diary number before you leave. Photograph it. Most common objection: missing court fee or an unnumbered annexure. Both are avoidable and both delay registration by days.

### How should a junior behave inside a courtroom?
Quietly, early and prepared: know your serial number, stand when your case is called, address the court with the correct title, and never interrupt another advocate.
Enter before the court sits and take a seat at the back, not at the bar table. Keep the file open at the last order, with the next date visible. Stand and state your appearance briefly: name, party and capacity. Never argue over another counsel's time. Wait your turn and ask politely for a pass. Write the order down as it is dictated. Do not rely on memory or on a later copy.

### What should you carry every day?
CNIC, bar card, vakalatnamas, court fee stamps, diary, cause list, pen, stapler, and the file for each matter listed that day.
Item Why CNIC and bar card Needed at the gate and for identification before a court Signed vakalatnamas You cannot appear without authority on the file Court fee stamps Applications are often filed at short notice Cause list copy Fast scanning when the court is already sitting Diary and two pens Orders are dictated, not emailed Stapler, tags, glue Files are assembled in the corridor, not the chamber

### How do you use the first month at City Courts well?
Attach yourself to one courtroom for a week, watch how matters are called, and record the phrases and steps you will need to copy.
Spend a full week in one courtroom and write down the daily routine. Learn how applications are moved: exemptions, adjournments, exhibits, orders. Collect the standard forms actually used by that court's office. Introduce yourself to the reader and the clerk — politely, once, with your name and chamber. Build a personal list of the ten phrases you must be able to say without thinking.

Q: Do I need a separate licence to appear at City Courts in Karachi?
A: A lower court advocate, licensed and enrolled through the provincial bar council, can appear before the civil and criminal courts. Confirm your own enrollment status with the Sindh Bar Council.

Q: Can a pupil appear in court alone?
A: A pupil appears with or under the supervision of the senior, in accordance with the chamber arrangement and the court's practice. Do not appear independently on a brief you are not authorised to handle.

Q: Where can I get copies of orders?
A: From the copying agency of the court concerned, on an application, once the order is on the file. Keep the receipt and follow up the same week.
